name: Middle part / curtains / textured crop trends

lead: Curtains are a long fringe divided by a middle or side parting, usually with shorter sides and back. Together with middle parts and textured crops they are among the men's cuts discussed as current, with curtains linked in recent years to K-pop artists. The payoff is a styled, up-to-date look from the moment you get the cut.

Fans say the fringe frames the face and covers the forehead or sides of the head. History sources trace curtains to early 20th century Britain with revivals since the 1980s. Looksmaxxing forum users debate which cuts flatter which facial proportions, and no studies test the effect on attractiveness.

paras: People grow the top out to fringe length, ask a barber for the cut, and style it with a bit of texture product or a blow-dry to set the part. Textured crops are cut shorter and styled with matte product. The look is visible right after the cut, and curtains take weeks of growth to reach.
No health risks are reported for the cuts themselves. Growing hair out takes time, and fringes need regular trims to keep their shape.

chain: Frames face with fringe or texture
angle.text: Middle parts, curtains and textured crops are current men's cuts, with curtains linked to K-pop artists. They frame the face with fringe or texture, and the new look is visible as soon as you have the cut. No studies test their effect on attractiveness.

lead: Middle parts, curtains and textured crops are men's haircuts used to change how the upper face reads. Curtains is a long fringe divided down the middle (or sometimes to one side) and falling either side of the face, with short or shaved sides and back.[1] A textured crop, also called a French crop, is a short cut with a choppy fringe brought forward over the forehead.[2] Haircuts are among the quickest, cheapest and most reversible ways to alter apparent facial proportions, and these cuts are chosen mostly for what they do around the forehead, temples and cheekbones.[2][3]

Grooming guides pair the cuts with face shapes and hairlines. Man of Many lists middle-part curtains for oval, round, square and triangle faces because the hair falls over the forehead, and a forward-styled French crop for oval, round and square faces, where the blunt fringe adds width to a longer face.[2] Looksmaxxing forum users make similar arguments, treating hair as a low-cost way to offset a perceived weak point such as narrow eye spacing, a high forehead or a weaker hairline.[4][5]

The look has a long history, from short curtained hair attributed to the Baiyue in the first millennium BCE, through early twentieth-century British working-class youth styles, to a late-1980s new wave revival, a 1990s peak worn by actors and musicians, and a 2020s return driven by TikTok, K-pop and 1990s nostalgia.[1][6][3] No clinical studies have tested these cuts.

paras: Curtained hair has a long fringe parted in the middle or at the side, with short or shaved sides and back.[1] The late-1980s centre-parted version derived from the bowl cut.[1] Ape to Gentleman distinguishes a centre-parted version, an off-centre or side-swept version, a longer shaggier version and an undercut version, and tells barbers to leave length on top, cut the back short and let the sides sit around the ears so the top and sides remain visibly separate.[7]

Man of Many lists further variants: the middle-part undercut with a long fringe over closely cut sides, short and long curtains, wavy curtains built on natural texture, faded curtains, a blunt-cut fringe, messy shaggy curtains with a 1970s feel, and a slicked 'e-boy' version in which the fringe stays forward and the rest is pushed back.[8] Wikipedia notes that e-boys, a TikTok-era youth style, often wear curtained hair.[9]

A textured crop keeps the sides short and styles a choppy, point-cut top forward over the forehead; Man of Many describes the French crop as needing a precise cut so the top and bottom halves of the head balance.[2] The related Caesar cut, named for Roman imagery of Augustus, has short fringe cut straight across the forehead and layering of about 2 to 5 cm all over, according to Wikipedia.[10] The bowl cut, a one-length cut with a straight fringe, was worn widely in medieval Europe and has been revived in recent decades.[11]

Man of Many recommends middle-part curtains for oval, round, square and triangle faces and says the parted hair falls like curtains and hides the forehead. It recommends the French crop for oval, round and square faces, saying a blunt forward fringe adds horizontal width to an elongated face and texture softens it.[2]

A separate Man of Many guide says rounder faces suit more height on top with tighter sides or a low-wedge fade, oval faces often suit a high taper, and longer faces suit softer curtains with less volume, and that a barber can shape the fringe around the cheekbones and jaw.[8]

The forehead guide defines a typical hairline as sitting about 7 to 8 cm above the point between the eyebrows, with a forehead over about 8 cm usually considered big. It adds that men with thick hair can use textured fringes to cover the forehead, whereas men with receding hairlines are better served by shorter, lower-volume cuts such as short fades or side-swept bangs, and that the Caesar cut is not suited to receding hairlines.[2]

The same guide quotes barber Lino D'Adderio on blending a fade to build weight at the temple and forehead, and editor Nick Hall on moving hair down and forward rather than up when covering a large forehead.[2] These pairings are the opinions of grooming writers and barbers; no controlled study of them is cited.

Ape to Gentleman says the style works for most hair types, is a poorer fit for very thin hair that lacks volume and for very tightly coiled hair, and that curly hair needs more length at the sides before it sits well.[7] It describes light waxes, creams or pomades, applying product mainly on wash days, dry shampoo to extend time between washes, blow-drying for control, and straightening irons or keratin treatments for unruly hair.[7]

Man of Many gives type-specific notes: blunt cuts and texture spray or matte paste for straight hair, sea-salt spray or cream for wavy hair, cutting curls to fall around the face for curly hair, removing bulk for thick hair, and light product for fine hair.[8] For textured crops it suggests texture powder or matte clay rather than heavy creams, point cutting on top for movement, and styling fringes forward and down.[2]

The Baiyue of the first millennium BCE appear to have worn short curtained hair.[1] In early twentieth-century Britain a long-on-top undercut variant was worn by working-class youth and street gangs such as Glasgow's Neds, Manchester's Scuttlers and Birmingham's Peaky Blinders; Glasgow Neds reportedly used paraffin wax to hold it, and the longer top is said to have been worn despite being a disadvantage in street fights.[1]

Ape to Gentleman traces the centre parting to the 1890s, noting Oscar Wilde's preference for it, and Man of Many describes a pomade-styled version in the 1920s that faded mid-century.[7][8] New wave and synthpop fans revived a centre-parted style in the late 1980s as an alternative to the mullets and backcombed hair of glam metal, and Brendan Fraser wore it in the 1990s.[1] Ape to Gentleman credits 1990s musicians and actors with the peak and grunge with a messier version.[7]

A 2025 YPulse report says the 1990s floppy centre-parted cut is returning among young men under the name 'curtains', appearing on TikTok and red carpets, compares it with 1990s figures such as Hugh Grant and Leonardo DiCaprio, and names actor Charles Melton and K-pop idols as current wearers. It attributes the revival to nostalgia and to young men's greater willingness to experiment with looks.[6] Wikipedia lists BTS, Monsta X and NCT members as K-pop associations.[1]

In February 2021 Capital FM described a TikTok trend in which Gen Z users labelled the side part a millennial habit and the middle part the youthful default, with users filming themselves switching parts; some millennials replied that the middle part was a 1990s style returning.[3] The e-boy aesthetic that emerged on TikTok in the late 2010s helped popularise curtained hair, with transformation videos becoming a feature of the subculture.[9]

Man of Many describes the slicked e-boy and the softer textured TikTok versions as popular variants, and Ape to Gentleman names Timothée Chalamet, Cillian Murphy, Robert Pattinson, Jimin of BTS and many 1990s figures among celebrities associated with curtains.[7][8]

Threads on looksmax.org compare curtains, fringe and other cuts. One poster argued that fringe or curtains suit everyone, pointing to pop and K-pop stars, and that curtains suit narrow eye spacing or weak cheekbones while fringe suits a poor hairline or forehead.[5] Another user asked whether curtains improve apparent interpupillary distance by covering bone lateral to the eyes, or reduce it by adding head width.[4] Other threads ask how to get the hair to lift at the centre part[12] and poll users on which cut ranks highest in a given year, with curtains and the wolf cut as candidates.[13]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hair is discussed as a low-cost way to adjust the apparent proportions of the upper face, and cuts are compared and polled by year.[4][5][13]
